blocks.x: I'd look and get your name down first and be good on you.
Jeanette Kimmel.
Again?
Jeanette Kimmel.
And what's today's date? 16th. June 16th.
1969. Jeanette, you came from past Christiane originally.
Born in Rio de Janeiro.
Did you have much of a family?
Yes, I had a white sister and two brothers.
What was your mother and father's name?
My mother was Susie Salmon. My father was Julius Salmon. S-A-L-B-N-T Salmon.
Were you, anybody in the family decisions?
Oh, no. Not in my immediate family. My sister took music lessons, but she was not as interested in it. Neither as talented.
But how did you become interested in music? I mean, what made you interested?

I always liked it from a child. My mother told me of how I would, when she would take me visiting, and if there was a piano, I would always get up on the stool and bang. So she said then she wanted me to have music lessons. And from that, and it was a tell, definitely, because I've always been interested in it. And my teacher couldn't keep me in music, in lessons.
What was the first band of music that you heard live? Do you remember? What kind of music was it?

Well, we had a lot of records as children, but I can't recall. But then the first band whom I heard as a child was Sam Morgan and Rainey, and at that bunch, they would come over there as a child. And they would barely own trucks around the home. And they would've been lost. I would've been lost. I think that was about the first.

Hey, Sam Morgan, for instance. Remember, did you carry a piano player, did he? I don't think so. I don't know. I don't know. I don't know. I don't know. I don't know. I don't know. What was the first band that you saw that was using a piano player?
Can I stop it for a second?
Excuse me.
They're talking about the piano player. First piano player. You can't remember that part? I just don't remember that part.

What was the... Can you remember any... Can you remember any straight bands, not jazz bands, that you heard around Paso Christiana? Were there all jazz bands or were there any straight orchestras playing out there?
No, it was a small town. There... Well, we used to play... I used to play with a little group over there, about four or five pieces, and we played just all types of music. Semi-classics and whatnot.
That was your first band? Yeah.
I was a child then.
Do you remember who played that then? Did you?
They all did. Eddie Watson, Harry Watson, a fellow playing bass named Murray. And another Watson playing banjoes. Stringes. No horns.
Who got the band together? Can you remember a little bit over there?

That small band? Yeah. Harry Watson was a leader. Oh, I see. He played mandolin. His brother, Eddie, played guitar. And the other brother, Henry, played banjoe. And this old man, Murray, played bass. And I can just a string of them. And we played for various entertainers, which was very nice.
Do you remember, when did you join Papa Subtame Band?
I joined his band in September 1926. Right out of high school.
Did they, I mean, how did they get in touch with you?
One of my friends over here heard that they wanted a pianist. And he recommended me. And they came over and interviewed me. And that's where it started.
What did, what, when you say that, who was it? Papa Subtame by himself? Papa Subtame and Paul Vaughn.
Oh.
I mean, what did they ask you?

Well, they found, they heard that I could read very well and was a good musician. Although I had never been away from home because I was too young to go away. And they came over and brought some orchestrations of which I had never seen, because I had only played sheet music. They brought some orchestrations and asked me to play them, and I played them right off. One of them I can remember as being Alabama Bound. That's the only one of which I can remember. And they asked my mother if I could join them. And she said, well, she's young, she's never been away from home, but I feel that she can take care of herself. And having a lot of relatives in New Orleans, she said, yes. So that's how I joined them.
What, were you in your teens then? Yeah. What, so you had to play for them. I mean, they didn't just talk to you. You actually had to play the piano for them.
Yes, I had to show them what I could do.
Okay. Who was in the band when you joined them? Can you remember?

Paul Vaughn, Mrs. Elliston, John Marrera, Simon Marrera, and a fellow playing trombone, and a trombone named Marr. Oh, I just can't think of his name now, but there was a trombone player. And I think that's, oh, at the time that I joined, it was a small group.
Was that, I mean, did they have a piano player in the band before you?
Yes, they said they had had Sweet Amel and several others.
So, so you weren't the first woman to play the band. Oh, yes. Was there, did you see many women playing piano with bands around here out of the... Yes.
Mercedes Fields, who is dead now, and Wilhelmina Bart, who is also dead, and a friend of mine, Ruby May Townsend, who is also dead, all three of whom I can remember.
Who do you remember as being one of your early influences on the piano? Can you remember anybody that you...
No, I just liked it. I didn't particularly take, you know, having one as an ideal. I just liked piano, liked music.
What kind of stuff would you have to play to the band, I mean, with Celestan's band? Just...

Well, we played, when we first started out, it was popular music. And then when we went into a large band, which was 14 pieces, then we played only arrangements. Strictly reading, all reading musicians. It was wonderful. We had a lovely large band.
What, even like the drums and the bass, they would all be reading too?
Oh, everybody was reading. We had to because we had special arrangements. We had writers in the band. Who was writing for the band. Yeah. And we had a wonderful society orchestra.
I mean, when you first joined the band, did they, did you just play the way you'd been playing, or did they want to change anything in your playing?

Well, I can't recall, but I knew I was playing music at that time. And I imagine I played... I always could improvise. So I imagine I was improvising then. But of course, it's a little different now because it's New Orleans Jazz. At that time, I think it was more music. Hmm.
I mean, you'd make four pieces of the measure mostly? Yeah, something like that.
And then of course when I would take solos, well then I would improvise. Yeah.
I see. Did you do any writing for the band? No, we had writers.
I didn't do any writing at all.
I think Paul Barnes wrote some things for the band, didn't he?
Oh, with that small band, yeah. And John Marrera. Of course, with the Lois Band, as I was saying, we had special writers. What kind of thing...
I mean, you played quite a long while with John Marrera, for instance. I mean...

Not too long. I imagine I played with John about two or three years, not longer than that. Because after that, Paul left town, I think, and John left town, and then there was a large... He created a large band. And then I stopped playing in 35 for 18 years. I didn't play with them anymore. I stopped in order to rear my family, because I married in 29. See, I joined in 26, I married in 29, and then I reared my family. After that, I stayed home to rear my family. I quit in 35. But during that time, I was still playing, but not regularly. Nor was I playing with them. I was playing... I was mostly teaching music then, in order to be home with my children, who were babies. And... I stayed out of the Celestine band for 18 years, and I rejoined in 53, and I've been there since. So there was an interim.

When you were playing with those early bands, like, say, the Celestine band with John Marrera, what did the banjo and the piano play together? I mean, did you both play the same chords all the while, or did you play on any different beats?
I think we played the same chords. We had to, in order to have the harmony right.
Yeah, I mean, did you both play fourth of measure, or...?

Well, he was a solo man a lot. He would play... I imagine he would play four, but of course he picked a lot. Picked beautifully, and when he would take a solo, he would begin picking. Then I would take the... the compliment. But I think... I can't recall too clearly, but I think he was a sort of four-four.
In other words, if you had to do a job where, say, John Marrera was sick, and there couldn't get anybody else, would you play differently than...
Oh, I would have to play four-four in order to give the beat along with the drum.
Yeah. Who was my drum with you then? You didn't have that, do you remember? Gosh.
I think it was Chinese. I think it was Chinese. It's been quite a long while, I guess I remember.
Did you hear him play when he came back, Chinese?
No, I didn't hear him when he came back.
Tell me, it was a very fast drummer.
He was very good at that time, yes.
What other piano players would you listen to about, at that time, around here?
One of my friends, whom I've mentioned, the pianist, the pianist whom I've mentioned, a farmer. I especially liked Ruby Mae Townsend, she was very good.
I've never heard of her, you know her, didn't she?

No. She wasn't too well known because she was a school teacher, but she was a very good pianist. She was a young man, and she did play with musicians sometimes. One of them being Minor, I think it was Minor, with whom she played. But she was very good. And she and I started taking music lessons at the same time. We were the most brilliant students I would teach at. So I know she was very good. But of course she was teaching school, and music was secondary with her.
I mean, were there any records that you were influenced by? I mean, did you hear any jazz records around that time that influenced you at all?

No, none of them influenced me. As I said, I didn't have anyone that I wanted to copy. I just liked music. I had no style that I wanted to copy. I just wanted my own. So therefore, no one influenced me really. I just liked music. It was a part of me, and it was my talent. And of course, as I say, I play all types. I didn't only play jazz. I play everything. So there was no one really influenced me.
What kind of a band did it with Celestine? I mean, was he a very good musician?
I think he was all right. A very likable person. He, he, what he did play, played well.
Why did he use two trumpets, you know, most of the time? Just...
Well, I imagine for harmony. They always had two trumpets.
I mean, even when you joined the band.
For harmony, you see, you always, in order to have everything sound right, you would have to have harmony. And one trumpet couldn't do it alone. You'd have to have first and second.
I know. Were there right parts where the trombone would harmonize with the trumpet?
Oh, yes. With a big band, they did that.
Yeah. Yeah. And the trombone would have started in the songs.
I think so. I can't recall too well about those things.
Well, we could listen to the records and see what it was.
Uh-huh. But I'm sure they had to have a harmony in order for it to sound right.
You make quite a few records in the twenties with Celestine.
Oh, about three or four.
Do you remember much about those recordings?
One was My Josephine. And other names that I just can't recall. John Marrera had several. And I was on those. That was when I first joined in 26, like I said.
Well, I think it was one, I forget the name of it, but he's featuring himself on the banjo. Yeah. Can I? I can't guess you'd plan on that.
Can you remember the name? Because I can't.
Uh, Station Calls. Oh, yes.
Station Calls. I remember that now.
Do you remember when those records came out? Did they send you a copy of those records when they came out?
I have them at my home in the Paschkechand. I have some of them. Uh-huh. They were made by Columbia, 78.
Did you hear much of Pierron's orchestra when you were young?

Yes, when I faced young, the orchestra, Pierron's orchestra was a society band here. They were very good, I heard them. And then after we organized a large band, we would meet them playing the different balls, because at that time we were playing the carnival balls. And Pierron's band and our band would be the bands of the night. And at the country club we would meet them quite often.
So they had quite a nice band?
Yes, it was a lovely, real society band.
Who was playing piano with them at that time?
Um, Alagretta Alexander, when I heard them, the first time I heard them was The Pianist Who's Dead Now. Maybe you know his name, Mr. Russell.
Was that before Steve Lewis?
Steve Lewis, the first one whom I heard once or twice, but he died shortly after. And then Alexander, Alagretta Alexander was a pianist most of the time after that.
Did most of the piano players around here, I mean, obviously they didn't play on the same style, but did they mostly play the same parts in a band?
Yes, when they were reading they had to play the same part, because everybody would improvise differently, I should imagine.
So most of the musicians that you came in contact with were reading musicians, really?
Yes, those with whom I played were all reading musicians. I haven't been with anyone other than reading musicians since I've been a musician.
Did you ever go around and hear Red Caillou or Toots or any of those people that were playing at parties?
No, I don't know Red Caillou.
You know Toots Washington?
No. Oh, yes, Isidore Washington?
Isidore Washington?
Oh, yes. Uh-huh. Yes, oh yes, he plays well.
I just wondered if, you know, he's told me about going to jam sessions, you know, that have the cutting contest between the two and the piano.
Well, he liked that, but I didn't like that. He didn't go around. I never did like jam sessions. But he plays by ear. Yes, he plays well by ear.
Do you remember much of the bands of King Oliver and the band of the... I didn't know them at all. Do you remember when Paul left and went to join?
I remember when Paul left because Paul was with us and he left.
Yeah. Mm-hmm. Who did, do you remember who saw Sam Gartman in this place?
A fellow who is in California now by the name of Pearson.
Oh, yeah. Did you hear your Fouche play?
Yes, I heard him in Sam Morgan's band as a child. He was playing with Sam Morgan at the time that I was given. He was very good.
Did he play anything like Paul? No? Was he that kind of a player or did he sound different from Paul?
Well, they were both very good. Of course they had their different styles. So I don't know, I couldn't say, but they were both very good. They were very good at that time on sax.
You never, you never remember any piano players playing with Sam Morgan's band?

No, I don't seem to be able to remember who was playing piano with Sam Morgan. Because I never could go to the dances. I was too young. I would just hear them as they were battling on the trucks. So I wasn't allowed to go to public dances. So I really don't know.
Yes, I always liked your singing and you won't sing anymore.

No, I can't sing anymore. I sang when we had a big band. I sang a lot when we were across the lake. But I have tonsillitis so I don't sing anymore. When I sing it, I start coughing. So therefore I just don't sing.
And you sang on one record then.
Yes, I sang on a record. I think it was one of Joe Moray's records. Dr. Sushan. Dr. Sushan had that session, yes.
You know, he studied under that Watson fellow. Who did? Dr. Sushan. Who did? Dr. Sushan. He did. Eddie watched the other day?
He did?
Yes. That's what he told me. I've seen his picture and all that. But you probably didn't know him.
I undoubtedly know him. I was over here then, I suppose, when he studied under Eddie. I didn't know that.
Well, that's when he was a little boy, so you wouldn't remember because he has a few years.
Well, Eddie was not that much older. Eddie, I had to be a boy too.
Well, they may have just played together as well.
Dr. Sushan. Undoubtedly, because Eddie was around his age.
Do you mind my asking, I hate to ask this question, but do you mind my asking your birthday?
I don't tell that. All right, you don't have to.
That's true. We don't want to ask that question. It just came out, because I know Dr. Sushan. I'll say this, I'm not that old.

You're not as old as Dr. Sushan. No, indeed. He never opened to me. I'm not that old. I don't consider myself an old person, which I am not that old, because I was young when I got married. I was young when I joined the band.
Fresh out of high school, you should.
And so, that's that.
Who were your teachers? Did you have many teachers?

I had various teachers, but the one to whom I give all credit was a Mrs. Stewart, because she gave me a foundation and a basic that one gets in college now. Transposition and Thoroughbass and Harmony, Theory, and all of that I had under her. And you don't get that until you advance, but she gave me a thoroughbass. So I give her all of the credit. I've had various teachers, but I give her the credit. And what's her full name? Her name is Mrs. Anna Stewart. She was a graduate of the New England Conservatory of Music. But she isn't playing anymore. Of course, she's old now. But she stopped quite some years ago. She was very good.
Is she still in the past?

No. I think she lives here. I'm not sure. But she moved from there after, oh, for quite a few years, quite a few years ago. And came over here to live. But I think she's back in the past, and I'm not too sure about where she's located. But she stopped playing. And stopped teaching also.
Did she play with bands? No.
She never did play with a band.
Solo only?
Just a music teacher. And a very good one.
And did you know August Russel? Russel?
August Russel was a trombone player whom I was trying to remember as being a part of the early band when I first joined. He was a trombone at that time. August Russel, yeah.
And what about the cornet player, Russelistan? Who was playing the second cornet?

When he had a big band is when he had the second cornet. That was Guy Kelly. But he didn't have a second cornet, I don't think. I can't recall him having a second cornet with a first band, I generally.
Did you ever play with Ricard and some of the songs?
Ricard played, I think I did, but I can't recall too clearly. I think I did at one time. It seems like he was playing bass, but maybe not. He might have been playing trumpet.
Well I know there are two cornets on its jam up, you know, Celestan and one other. And I didn't know.
Well I don't know who it was.
You don't remember who they were. You haven't heard the records. It could be Ricard, it could be Guy Kelly.
It might have been. I doubt if it was Guy Kelly because he hadn't come in the picture then. He hadn't. He joined in when he had the big band. So it wasn't Guy Kelly, it might have been Ricard.
You know, he had various singers, men that would sing on the records too.
Yes.
Does Charny sing on, Papa's Got the Jim Jams? I think he's supposed to sing on one of them, yeah. And then Frog's brother, what's his name, Ferdinand Joseph?
Well Ferdinand sang on one, yeah. And then there was another fella, Charlie, somebody who sang on another.
Charles Gills. Yeah. Charles Gills. Yeah.
Yes. Did you travel out of town much with Celesteiner?
Yes.
I traveled quite a bit with him, with the big band.
How far would you go?
I didn't mind it then because I had a husband in the band. So it didn't matter too much traveling then, I was in the 30s. We went all over the south.
And how old was your oldest child? When was the oldest child?
My oldest child was 36.
So this is 60, huh? So could you travel after your child was born?

I traveled a little bit after they were born and then I decided I was going to stop. That's when I stopped. And my mother kept them for me while I was gone. But I stopped because it was just too much and I wanted to be with my children myself. So I stopped all together.
Could you tell us a little bit about a carnival ball? What it's like?
Frankly, I don't, I wasn't too interested in the ball itself. I was more interested in the music. So I really couldn't give any information on the ball.
Well I just wondered what kind of music you'd play at a ball for example.
Well we had to play Aida and things like that for the Grand March and then we played our arrangements of which we had at that time. Different numbers that we had specially arranged.
Would you play for Rex, Pumas, Mamas? All those. All the big clubs.
They were held at that, that's the name of the band.
When somebody, when you replaced somebody in Celestan's band, did you all get together and discuss what you should bring in the band? Or did Celestan just hire the people anyway?

Well, he would hire the replacements whenever there was an opening. I mean if anybody had to lay off or something like that he would hire a replacement but it would be someone who could read and use it.
I mean did he ever ask all of your people in the band who you wanted or who you wanted?
No, he would hire who he wanted himself.
And he always kept the banjo and piano?
Did he always select them?
No, did he always keep the two banjo and piano or did sometimes he just work with the piano?
Well, at the time he would have both banjo and piano, most of the time.
I mean when John Marrera went up to New York or something like that?

Well after that time I think he formed the big band and then my husband was the one who would play banjo. He was my husband at that time when he first joined but then afterward he was the one who would banjo play in the band. Then he had several, I think he had several others before he came in. That would fill in but as a regular man that was the one.
What were some of the classics that you played yourself, either alone or with the band?
Well with the band I didn't play classics. But alone I played all of the classics because I played for a dance review. I still play for this dance review and I have to play all types of music.
Well what are some of the names of them?
stuff because it's in seven sharps.
Mm.
Mm. And a lot of Chopin's music, and Bach and Rachmaninoff, all of that, especially for this dancer, you've got to play all that type of stuff. Mm-hmm.
Any questions, Rob? I have one more. Who were some of the arrangers that wrote for Celestan?

There was a fellow from St. Louis who was very good by the name of Cecil. I can't remember his last name right now, but Cecil was one who was hired especially for arranging. Then there was one named Henry Holloway. Kildee. Kildee. Kildee. He was a member of the band. He was very good as an arranger. And we used to buy arrangements from Fats Pichon.
So he used to write arrangements?
Oh, he was, yes. He was a very good arranger. And he used to buy arrangements from various people, but these three were outstanding as arrangers.
He didn't use stock arrangements, no?
We used stock, but we would especially run. Yes, add some more courses. Yeah, yeah.
He is some stock, but mostly specials.
What about Adolf Alexander Sr., did you ever play any of his arrangements? No, not Tats, but his father.
I didn't know his father.
I just wondered. Did you know a fellow named Thornton that wrote arrangements? He played saxophone, played tenor, I think, from out of St. Louis.
Cecil Thornton, that's the fellow of whom I'm speaking. Very good arrangement.
What about these two sawstand bands that he had, do you know? Remember in the 50s?
Well, I wasn't with them then, so I don't know anything about that. Well, didn't you come back? I came back in 53. Yes, but he had... He didn't have two bands then. He had them before.
Well, I know he had one band at the paddock. You don't know...
I wasn't with them in that year. I hadn't come back then.
I never did quite understand that, because I'd seen him sometimes, I think he had Mercedes.
Well, I wasn't that... I was out then. I wasn't there with them.
What were some of the earliest piano copies, you know, sheet music for piano that you ever played?
My Gal Sal was one. That was my first piece of sheet music that I ever attempted as a child.
Any others you remember from back then?
That's the only one I was really interested in, because I was so happy that I could play.
Did you play by ear before you took any lessons? No. Always... you started off with music but could always...
Yeah, seven years old. I started my first lesson.
And who did you play with after you quit Solishten in 35? Would you play in any little spots or what?

I played... I was doing mostly teaching then, but in the 40s I played with Leary's orchestra for about... I think from 49 to 53 when I joined, rejoined the Solishten group. And then from 46 to 49 I was playing at the Dewdrop nightclub.
